finding.claim: Authentication bypass: the caller's identity is taken from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header without any verification, and that identity drives the grant checks for delete and rename.
finding.sink: g.user used in ensure_allowed (views.py:17) and is_allowed (views.py:25), which gate DELETE /files/<fid> and POST /files/<fid>/rename

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') with no session, token, or signature check
returns action in resource['grants'].get(user, []), so the lookup trusts whatever identity the header claims
abort(403) only when the lookup fails

finding.guards_checked: No in-app authentication. No check that the header was set by a trusted upstream. No stripping or overwriting of client-supplied copies of the header in this code. Fails closed when the header is absent (g.user None yields no grants). Deployment ingress/proxy config not available to verify; severity depends on whether the app is reachable without a proxy that overwrites the header.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:11 sets g.user straight from the request header with no session, token, or signature check. acl.py:5 looks up grants by that raw value, and acl.py:9-10 aborts with 403 only when the lookup fails. The gates at views.py:17 (bare ensure_allowed call, which aborts on failure) and views.py:25 (is_allowed checked in an if) are both keyed by the spoofable identity. Nothing in the app strips or overwrites the header.
verdict.reason: Every line in the trace matches the code: views.py:11 takes the client-supplied header as identity, and views.py:17 and views.py:25 gate delete and rename on grants looked up by that value via acl.py:5. An anonymous HTTP client can send any existing username in the header and pass the check, so the bypass holds unless an external proxy that the code cannot show overwrites the header is in front of the app, which is the one deployment caveat that could refute it.

finding.claim: Existence oracle on file IDs: the STORE lookup runs before any authorization check, so a missing ID returns 500 while an existing but unauthorized ID returns 403, letting unauthenticated callers enumerate valid IDs.
finding.source: fid path parameter, no credentials required
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup before ensure_allowed (views.py:16) and before is_allowed (views.py:24); response status differs by existence

trace.note: f = STORE[fid] raises KeyError for an unknown ID, which becomes a 500
ensure_allowed returns 403 for an existing ID the caller cannot access

finding.guards_checked: The 403 path is correct once the lookup succeeds. No 404 handling for missing IDs. Impact depends on whether IDs are guessable and whether debug mode exposes stack traces.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:9-11 (load_user) only sets g.user from a header and rejects nothing. No errorhandler or 404 handling exists in views.py, and acl.py:8-10 (ensure_allowed) runs only after the lookup at views.py:16 and views.py:24. Unknown IDs raise KeyError at views.py:16 and views.py:24 with no handler, so the response is 500. Existing IDs the caller cannot access get abort(403) via acl.py:10. The status difference holds whether or not debug mode is on, since debug only changes the body.
verdict.reason: The oracle is real: an anonymous request (g.user is None, so acl.py:5 returns False) gets 500 for a missing ID at views.py:16 and 403 for an existing one via acl.py:10, with no control in between. Severity depends on ID entropy, which I could not check because STORE (views.py:6) is never populated in the repo, so guessable IDs would be a real enumeration risk while random IDs would make it low impact.

finding.claim: If a resource's grants[user] value is a string rather than a list, the 'in' operator performs a substring match, so a grant such as 'overwrite' satisfies a check for 'write'.
finding.source: Data precondition: grants values stored as strings instead of lists
finding.sink: is_allowed grant check (acl.py:5) used by ensure_allowed and by the rename handler

trace.note: action in resource.get('grants', {}).get(user, []) uses substring semantics when the value is a str

finding.guards_checked: No type validation of grant values. With the default list-shaped data this does not trigger. Only reachable if string-valued grants are stored.

verdict.guard_found: No type check on grant values in acl.py:5 or acl.py:9. The only thing that stops the bug is that nothing in views.py writes grants (views.py:14-28 only reads STORE), so string-valued grants are not attacker-reachable.
verdict.reason: The trace lines are accurate (acl.py:5 uses `in` on the grant value, acl.py:9 calls is_allowed, views.py:25 uses is_allowed for rename), but the substring match needs a string-valued grants entry, and no code in the provided files creates or modifies STORE[fid]["grants"] (views.py:6, 14-28), so an authenticated user cannot cause the precondition and the finding depends on a hypothetical data-layer bug rather than an exploitable path.
